title: What a closure captures
prompt_md: A closure captures the *variable*, not the value it held when the closure was created. That one sentence explains every result below: work through them before revealing the answers.

questions.stem_md:
```python
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
```
What is printed?
questions.explanation_md: Each lambda captures the variable `i`, not its value at creation time. The lambdas do not run until the second line, by which point the loop has finished and `i` is `2`. So all three read `2`. The functions were never different from one another.

sources.locator: Why do lambdas defined in a loop return the same result?

questions.stem_md:
```python
funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
```
What is printed, and why is this different from the previous one?

options.md: `[0, 1, 2]`: `i=i` binds the *current value* as a default at each iteration.
`[2, 2, 2]`: the default does not change anything.
`SyntaxError`: you cannot name a default after the free variable.

questions.explanation_md: Default arguments are evaluated when the `lambda` is created, so `i=i` snapshots the loop value into a per-lambda parameter. Here the mutable-default trap (evaluate-once) is exactly what you want: it converts a late-bound free variable into an early-bound default. It is a common fix, though a factory function reads more clearly.

questions.stem_md:
```python
def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def tick():
        n += 1
        return n
    return tick

make_counter()()
```
What happens?

options.md: `UnboundLocalError`: `n += 1` makes `n` local to `tick`, so the read has no value yet.
Returns `1`; the closure updates `n` in the enclosing scope.

questions.explanation_md: Assigning to `n` anywhere in `tick` makes `n` a local of `tick` for the whole function, so `n += 1` reads a local that has not been assigned yet. Reading a closed-over variable is fine; *rebinding* it needs `nonlocal n`. (Mutating a captured mutable object, e.g. `counts[0] += 1`, needs no declaration because it rebinds nothing.)

questions.stem_md:
```python
def outer(a):
    b = a * 2
    def inner(c):
        return a + b + c
    return inner
```
Which names are free variables of `inner` (captured from the enclosing scope)?
questions.explanation_md: A free variable is one used in `inner` but bound in an enclosing function. `a` and `b` qualify; `c` is `inner`'s own parameter (local), and `inner` is a local of `outer`. You can see the captured set at runtime via `inner.__code__.co_freevars` and the live cells via `inner.__closure__`.

sources.locator: Execution model: binding of names, free variables

questions.stem_md:
```python
def make_pair():
    x = 0
    def get(): return x
    def inc(): nonlocal x; x += 1
    return get, inc

get, inc = make_pair()
inc(); inc()
print(get())
```
What is printed?

options.md: `2`: both closures share the same cell for `x`.
`0`: each closure has its own copy of `x`.

questions.explanation_md: `get` and `inc` close over the *same* variable `x` from the one `make_pair` call, so they share state through a single cell. This is the basis of the closure-as-object pattern: several functions sharing private state without a class. Call `make_pair` again and you get a fresh, independent `x`.

sources.locator: Data model: cell objects hold closure variables

hints.md: The governing rule: a closure captures the variable, and reads it when the closure is *called*, not when it is created. So a loop variable read after the loop is its final value.

Two consequences. To freeze a value at creation time, use a per-function default (`i=i`) or a factory that takes the value as an argument. And to *rebind* a captured variable inside the inner function you need `nonlocal`; merely reading it, or mutating an object it points to, does not.
Answers: (1) `[2, 2, 2]`. (2) `[0, 1, 2]`: `i=i` snapshots each value. (3) `UnboundLocalError`: needs `nonlocal n`. (4) free variables are `a` and `b`. (5) `2`: the two closures share one cell.
